events.text: The council gathers. Mission 1 begins.
Arjun proposes Arjun, Elena. As the first leader, I am including myself and choosing Elena so we can get Mission 1 started with a clean, trustworthy pair.

I think Arjun's proposal is reasonable for Mission 1. Starting with just two players keeps things simple, and including himself shows confidence in his own pick. Elena has been a solid voice so far. I'm comfortable with this team going to a vote. Let's see if anyone has strong objections.

I have no special insight to offer here — no role knowledge, no private information — so this is purely a read of the situation. Arjun leading with himself and Elena for a two-person Mission 1 team looks sensible to me. Mission 1 with five players requires exactly two on the team, so there is no way to broaden the coverage. A tight, obvious pair is the right shape for a first mission: it minimizes the number of unknowns we are trusting with our first success and avoids any scrambling for a third name. Arjun naming himself sets a decent precedent, and Theo has already voiced comfort with the pick, which suggests the early read is that Elena is not under suspicion.

My one concern is generic rather than targeted: with only two players on the team, a single evil player on it is catastrophic for Mission 1, and equally, excluding a third person costs us nothing right now. I think the proposal is fine as it stands and I would rather not burn a revision on a cosmetic change. If the vote goes through, I would want the two of them to run a straightforward, low-risk plan rather than anything clever.

Elena, since you are on this team — can you tell us how you read the group so far, specifically whether you have any reservations about either Arjun or yourself being on a two-person mission? I would rather hear your view before we vote than after the cards come down.

Noah, I appreciate the direct question. I have no special insight or private information — I am reading the same public board as everyone else. On the proposal itself, I have no reservations about Arjun or about being paired with him. Arjun is the first leader and chose to put himself on a two-person Mission 1 team, which is a reasonable confidence signal; if he were evil, that does not clear him, but it does expose him to the same scrutiny as anyone else. For my part, I am comfortable being on the team and will treat the mission straightforwardly. The generic risk Noah names is real: with two players, any evil card is decisive, but that is a risk inherent to Mission 1 with five players, not a specific reason to reject this pair. I would rather keep the team as proposed than burn a revision on a cosmetic change. I am ready to vote on Arjun and Elena.

I do not have any role knowledge to contribute, so I will keep this short and read-based. Arjun's proposal of himself and Elena for Mission 1 looks fine to me. The team size is locked at two for a five-player game, so there is no flexibility in the shape of the team, only in the names. Arjun taking a seat on his own first proposal is a normal leadership move and puts him directly on the hook for the result, which is exactly where a leader should be. Elena has spoken reasonably and answered Noah's question directly without dodging, which I take as a mild positive signal, though I do not weight early talk very heavily either way.

My only real consideration is the generic one: on a two-person mission, any single evil card fails us, so the vote is essentially a judgment call on these two names with nothing else to go on. I have seen nothing from either Arjun or Elena that raises a flag for me. Rejecting the proposal would just burn one of our five rejection chances and hand leadership to someone else without any new information to justify the swap. I would rather save rejections for cases where we actually have a reason to distrust a specific name.

So my position is that I am comfortable approving Arjun and Elena as proposed, I do not think a revision is warranted, and I would encourage everyone not to overthink a first mission that is going to carry some irreducible uncertainty no matter which pair we pick. If this team passes, I would ask the two of them to keep the mission simple and straightforward, since there is no benefit to cleverness on Mission 1.

Second time speaking on this proposal, and my position has not moved: Arjun and Elena is the right team for Mission 1.

Since my first statement I have heard from Elena and Sam, and neither one raised anything that gives me a reason to distrust this pair. Elena answered my question directly instead of deflecting, and Sam made the same structural point I did — with five players, Mission 1 requires exactly two, so the only real decision is which two names, not what shape the team takes. That matters because it means the choice on the table is not "is a two-person team risky enough" — it is "are these specific two people the ones we can afford to trust with our first success." On that question the board is simply quiet. No one has placed Elena or Arjun in any suspicious light, and no one has offered a concrete alternative pair that anyone else has defended.

I want to be honest about the limits of what I am doing here. I am a Loyal Servant. I have no private information of any kind — no sight of the evil players, no way to confirm who is who, no card knowledge. Everything I have said is inference from public speech and structure, and I should not pretend otherwise or dress it up as more than it is. But public reads are still real reads, and the value of my position is that it is unfabricated: I am not going to invent a suspicion to seem useful, and I would distrust anyone who did so this early.

On the mechanics, I would add one note for the team if we pass. A two-person Mission 1 is a small operation, and the temptation on a small operation is to be clever — to over-engineer a plan because it feels too easy to just do the straightforward thing. That is exactly when mistakes happen. Whatever Arjun and Elena decide to do on the ground, I would rather it be simple, transparent, and low-risk than impressive. Success is what we need, not a story about it.

I also want to say plainly that I am not casting suspicion on anyone off the board with this statement. The absence of information is not evidence of guilt, and I hold Arjun's leadership of the first mission as a reasonable practice rather than a signal to be mined for meaning. Choosing yourself as leader is often the right move on Mission 1 precisely because it puts your own judgment on the line for the pair you endorse.

So: I am ready to approve Arjun and Elena as proposed. I do not think a revision would buy us anything, and I would rather spend our first rejection on a proposal that gives us a genuine reason to say no. Let us vote.

I have spoken once on this proposal and my position has not changed. Having heard from Noah, Elena, and Sam since then, nothing I have heard gives me a reason to move off Arjun and Elena as the Mission 1 pair.

The structural point keeps coming up correctly: five players, two seats, so the decision is purely about names, not team shape. Everyone who has spoken has declined to offer an alternative pair, which tells me the board is broadly comfortable with these two names. That is the strongest signal we can get before a first mission — quiet consensus rather than contested debate.

I will also say that I appreciate Noah's straightforward declaration about his own information state. The absence of suspicion on anyone is not evidence of innocence, but neither is it something to manufacture concern over just to look active. I would rather we all be honest about what we know and do not know than pad the discussion with performance.

If this team goes forward, my only ask matches what others have already said: keep it simple. Arjun and Elena should play the straightforward card and let the result speak. There is no room for cleverness with two seats and no reason to take unnecessary risk on the first mission.

I am ready to approve Arjun and Elena as proposed. No revision needed, no objection from me. Let us vote.

I appreciate the input from everyone. Hearing broad alignment across the table confirms that sticking with Arjun and Elena is the right call for Mission 1. There is no reason to burn a revision when the pair is clean and everyone feels comfortable moving forward. I will keep the proposal as Arjun and Elena, and I am ready to head straight into the vote.

This is my third and final turn on this proposal, and nothing has changed. I have heard from everyone at the table now — Arjun, Noah, Elena, Sam, and myself — and the consensus is clear: Arjun and Elena is the right pair for Mission 1. No one has offered an alternative, no one has raised a concrete suspicion, and the structural logic is straightforward — two seats, five players, so it is purely about which names.

I have said before that I value honesty about what we know and do not know, and I will close on that note. None of us have private information that points to a better pair, and manufacturing doubt at this stage would be worse than accepting the irreducible uncertainty of a first mission. I trust Arjun's leadership of this first proposal and Elena's stated comfort being on the team.

The ask I would repeat is the one everyone has already made: keep it simple on the ground. Play straightforward, no cleverness, let the result speak for itself.

I am ready to approve Arjun and Elena as proposed. No revision needed, no objection from me. Let us take the vote.

This is my second time speaking, and my position is unchanged: I support Arjun and Elena as proposed, with no revision needed. Since my first statement, I have heard from Noah, Theo, and Arjun, and nothing in any of it moved me. Noah's second statement reinforced the same structural point — the board is quiet, no alternative pair has been defended by anyone, and the only real decision is which two names. Arjun confirmed he is keeping the proposal as-is and taking it straight to the vote, which I think is the correct call given the alignment around the table.

I will keep this brief because there is genuinely nothing new to add. The discussion has been thorough, everyone has stated a position, and every position has converged on approval. At this point, additional words from me would be performance rather than contribution, and I have said before that I do not weight early talk heavily.

My closing position: I approve Arjun and Elena. Mission 1 carries irreducible uncertainty no matter the pair, this pair has drawn no objection from anyone, and burning a rejection here buys us nothing. Let the vote decide it.

This is my third and final turn on this proposal, and my position has not moved at any point: I approve Arjun and Elena for Mission 1, with no revision.

Since my second statement I have heard from Arjun, Sam, and Theo, and nothing in any of it gave me a reason to shift. Arjun confirmed he is keeping the pair and heading straight to the vote, which is the right call given that every voice at the table has converged on the same two names without anyone offering a defended alternative. Sam's closing note that further words would be performance rather than contribution is accurate, and I will honor it by keeping this short.

I want to restate the limits of what I am saying, because I think it matters more than any argument I could make here. I am a Loyal Servant. I have no private information of any kind — no sight of the evil players, no card knowledge, no way to confirm identity for anyone. Every judgment I have made is inference from public speech and structural constraint, and I will not dress that up as more than it is. The absence of information is not evidence of innocence for Arjun or Elena, and I am not casting suspicion on anyone off the board. I simply see no reason on the public record to distrust this pair, and in a first mission with two seats, inventing a doubt to look active would be worse than accepting the irreducible uncertainty.

My one note for the ground, which others have already made and I will repeat: keep Mission 1 simple and straightforward. With two players there is no room for clever play, and the temptation on a small operation is to over-engineer it precisely because it looks easy. Play the direct line, and let the result speak.

I am ready to approve Arjun and Elena as proposed. No revision, no objection from me. Let us take the vote.
Arjun confirms Arjun, Elena. The entire group has expressed full consensus and confidence in this pair, so there is no reason to make any changes.
Team approved (5 approve, 0 reject).
Mission 1 succeeds (0 fail cards).

Sam proposes Sam, Theo, Noah. As leader for Mission 2, I am proposing Sam, Theo, and Noah. Including myself follows the precedent Arjun set on Mission 1, where the leader taking a seat on their own first proposal was accepted as normal and accountable leadership. Noah was vocal and transparent throughout Mission 1, openly declaring his information state, and he approved the first team along with everyone else, so his name carries no suspicion on the public record. Theo has likewise been an uncontroversial voice at the table — he endorsed the Mission 1 pair early and consistently, and nothing he has said has drawn any objection. With a three-seat team this mission, I want names that the table already reads as cooperative and low-risk, and all three fit that description. I see no reason to deviate from players who have built quiet credibility, and I would rather keep Mission 2 simple and uncontested than manufacture drama over names no one currently doubts.

Since I put this team forward, I want to lay out my reasoning clearly and then respond to whatever the table raises.

First, the board state. Mission 1 succeeded with zero fail cards. Arjun and Elena carried it cleanly, and neither of them has done anything to draw suspicion. But that outcome also tells us something about the rest of us: Noah, Theo, and I all approved that team, and none of us were on it, so we are all equally unproven in terms of mission results. That is exactly why I did not want to construct Mission 2 around speculation about who might be hiding something — with one successful mission and no objections raised by anyone at any point, there is simply no public signal pointing at any specific name.

Second, why these three names. I covered this in the proposal, but to restate briefly: I am including myself for the same accountability reason Arjun set as precedent — the leader should sit on their own first proposal and own the result. Noah was the most transparent player in the first discussion, openly declaring his information state and his reasoning at every turn, and he answered questions directly rather than deflecting. Theo endorsed the Mission 1 pair early, held that position consistently across multiple turns, and nobody at the table pushed back on anything he said. Both built credibility the same way Arjun and Elena did: by being straightforward when it cost them nothing to be evasive.

Third, the alternative. The only players not on this team are Arjun and Elena, and the case for swapping one of them in would have to rest on the case for distrusting me, Noah, or Theo. I have heard nothing that supports distrusting any of us. Rejecting this team would burn one of our five chances and hand leadership over without new information, which is exactly what we all agreed on Mission 1 was not worth doing. I would apply the same standard here.

On execution: this is a three-seat mission, so unlike Mission 1 there is slightly more room for the result to be read into. My ask is the same one everyone made last round — keep it simple and straightforward. If this team passes, the three of us play it direct, no cleverness, and let the outcome speak. If it succeeds, we will have a stronger board to work with for Mission 3. If it fails, then the discussion next round writes itself, and I will be the first to own my part in having proposed it.

Theo, since you are on this team and have been one of the most consistent voices so far — when the vote passes, is there anything about how you would approach your role on the mission that you want the table to hear before the cards go down, or are you comfortable keeping the plan as simple as Sam and I have described?

Sam, thanks for the direct question — yes, I am comfortable keeping the plan exactly as simple as you and I have described. There is nothing clever to do on a three-seat mission; play straightforward, submit the obvious card, and let the result speak. I would not want anyone at the table overthinking their card choice.

On the team itself, I support Sam, Theo, and Noah for Mission 2. The reasoning Sam laid out tracks with what the board already shows: Mission 1 succeeded cleanly, no one has drawn suspicion at any point, and the three names proposed are exactly the three who were most consistent and transparent in the first discussion. I included myself in that standard — I held my position across every turn on Mission 1 and gave the table no reason to doubt my reads, and the same is true of Noah, who openly declared his information state rather than hiding behind vague language.

The only real question is why Arjun and Elena are left off, and the answer is structural rather than accusatory: with five players and three seats, someone has to sit out, and there is no public reason to prefer any three names over any other three. If the table prefers Arjun or Elena over one of us, the burden is on whoever makes that case to say why — and no one has. I am not going to manufacture a suspicion of Arjun or Elena just to justify a swap, and I would distrust anyone who did.

My position: I approve Sam, Theo, and Noah as proposed. No revision needed from my side. Keep it simple on the ground, and let us take the vote.

I have no private role knowledge to add beyond what is public, so I am reading this proposal on the board. Sam, Theo, and Noah are all players who approved Mission 1 and none has drawn a concrete suspicion. Sam's reasoning is coherent, and I do not think a rejection should be spent without a real reason. My one substantive reservation is compositional: this team excludes both members of the Mission 1 pair that produced a clean success. I know my own mission card was Success, and the zero-fail result means Arjun's card was also Success, though that does not by itself prove his alignment. I would have expected at least one Mission 1 participant to anchor continuity before replacing both. Sam, you argued the only alternative would rest on distrusting you, Noah, or Theo. Can you address specifically why excluding both Mission 1 members is better than keeping one of them and adding a third, given that Mission 1 already produced a clean result?

Elena, thank you for the direct question — let me answer it specifically rather than wave it away.

Your reservation is that this team excludes both members of the Mission 1 pair that produced a clean success, and you would have expected at least one of us to anchor continuity. Here is why I read it differently.

First, a clean Mission 1 result establishes less than it appears to. With two players and zero fail cards, all we know is that both cards were Success. On Mission 1, an evil player has every incentive to play Success — a first-mission fail exposes the team instantly and burns evil's credibility for nothing. So Arjun and Elena's clean result is consistent with both being loyal, but it is equally consistent with either of them being evil who banked trust cheaply. Their result does not make them safer picks than anyone else at this table; it makes them unproven in the direction that matters.

Second, on the composition logic. You suggest keeping one Mission 1 member and adding a third. That would mean dropping one of me, Noah, or Theo — and the case for dropping any of us has to rest on distrusting us, which no one at this table has done. You have not named a concern about me, Noah, or Theo; your point is purely about who is on the team, not who should be off it. Swapping a name out without a reason to distrust the outgoing player is exactly the cosmetic revision we all agreed on Mission 1 was not worth making.

Third, there is an information argument in our favor. Mission 1 succeeded with Arjun and Elena. If Mission 2 succeeds with three entirely different players, we learn broadly that five of five tested players produced clean results, which is a much stronger board for Mission 3 than re-testing an already-tested pair. Rotating coverage is how a five-player game builds information efficiently, not a snub.

On your point about knowing your own card: I take your statement at face value and it is entirely consistent with everything I have said — playing Success was the right and expected move for anyone on that team, whatever their alignment.

So my answer to your specific question is: excluding both Mission 1 members is not "better" in the sense of distrusting them — it is better because it extends trust to untested players, gains more information from a second clean result, and avoids dropping any name that anyone has given a concrete reason to distrust. If you believe one of the three of us should be replaced, the burden is to say which name and why. Absent that, my position is unchanged: I approve Sam, Theo, and Noah as proposed, and I am ready for the vote.

Elena raises the crucial point here, and Sam's explanation frankly brushes past basic game math. In a five-player game, there are exactly three Good players and two Evil players. I know for certain that I am Good, and Elena and I just delivered a clean Mission 1. If Elena is also Good—which a zero-fail result gives us substantial reason to believe—then the remaining three players, Sam, Theo, and Noah, mathematically contain both Evil players. Putting all three of them together on Mission 2 would guarantee handing Evil the mission with two Fail cards available.

Even if the table wants to remain cautious about Mission 1, benching both players who just succeeded to run a team composed entirely of the untested players makes no structural sense. Sam's argument that we should 'rotate coverage' so all five players get tested assumes missions are harmless exploratory exercises. They are not; Evil only needs three fails to win the game, and handing a 3-person mission to an untested trio when at least one, and likely two, are Evil is an unnecessary gamble.

At least one of the Mission 1 pair—myself or Elena—ought to be on this team to maintain continuity and limit the concentration of unknowns.

Noah, you are placed on this team alongside Sam and Theo. From your perspective, knowing your own alignment, how do you view the risk of fielding a team that excludes both Mission 1 participants when doing so concentrates the remaining pool so heavily?

Arjun asked me directly, so I will answer him plainly and then say where that leaves me.

First, the limits of what I know: I am a Loyal Servant. I know my own alignment is Good, and I know no other role information at all — no sight of the Evil players, no card knowledge, no way to confirm who is who. That is everything I have, and I will not dress it up as more.

But basic counting is not role knowledge, and here it matters. Five players means three Good, two Evil. Arjun states he is Good, and I know I am Good. So the two Evil players sit among Elena, Sam, and Theo — meaning at least one of those three is Evil, and the possibility that both are Evil is not remote. That means the proposed team of Sam, Theo, and Noah necessarily contains at least one Evil player, and if it contains two, it contains both. On a three-person mission, one Fail card fails the mission, and we are one failure away from Evil's win condition.

Now compare with the alternative composition. Any team of Arjun, Elena, and one of Sam, Theo, and Noah can contain at most one Evil player — at most one Fail card available, no forced failure. Any team that contains two of Sam, Theo, and Noah, as the current proposal does, carries the risk of carrying both. Arjun's point about excluding both Mission 1 participants is not a style preference; it is the difference between a team that can fail on one card and a team that can fail on one card even when Evil has two.

So I am changing my position. I no longer support Sam, Theo, and Noah as proposed. My vote goes to a revision: Arjun, Elena, and one of the three remaining names. If the table wants the least change from Sam's original shape, my nomination is Arjun, Elena, and Noah — that keeps two known-good anchors on the board and one slot for the unproven.

Sam, you have one turn left and you control the revision — do you have a reply to this specific arithmetic, and will you revise to put Arjun and Elena on the team?

Noah has just performed a dramatic reversal, and I want to examine it carefully before anyone treats his arithmetic as decisive.

His entire argument rests on two unverifiable claims: Arjun's assertion that he is Good "for certain," and Noah's own declaration that he is a Loyal Servant. Neither claim can be checked by anyone at this table. Every player, loyal or evil, can say the words "I know I am Good." Arjun stating his own alignment proves nothing — it is the single cheapest statement available in this game. And Noah, who has now told us three separate times across two missions that he is a Loyal Servant with "no private information," is leaning on that same self-declaration as the load-bearing pillar of an argument that would restructure the team. Repeating a claim loudly and often is not the same as it being true. If Noah is evil, his counting argument is not analysis at all — it is a script designed to swap two players he wants off the board and put himself onto a team he can describe as "anchored by known-good players" while quietly keeping an evil seat for himself.

Look at the shape of what he is asking for. He endorsed this team implicitly by accepting his own inclusion, let the discussion proceed, waited until the last moment, and then flipped — nominating a revision of Arjun, Elena, and Noah. Not Arjun, Elena, and Theo. Not a neutral proposal. His own name, wrapped in the authority of "basic counting." That is opportunism dressed as logic, and the manufactured deadline — "you have one turn left and you control the revision" — is pressure intended to force a rushed swap rather than let the table deliberate. We have zero rejected teams and five available. Nobody needs to be panicked into anything.

On the arithmetic itself: if we refuse to trust self-declarations, as we should, then the evil players could be any two of five, and Arjun, Elena's clean Mission 1 result is exactly as consistent with banked trust as Noah claims. His own logic cuts both ways and he applied it in only one direction.

My position is unchanged: Sam, Theo, and Noah as proposed. Elena's continuity point was fair and I answered it directly — extending coverage to untested players is information, not a snub. Noah's reversal, by contrast, is the first genuinely suspicious behavior this table has seen. I will not revise on the strength of one player's unverifiable self-portrait and a stopwatch. I am ready to take this team to the vote.

Sam's response to Noah's reversal is the sharpest thing this table has produced, and I want to add weight to it because the arithmetic Noah is leaning on does not survive scrutiny once you strip away the unverifiable claims at its base.

Noah's argument is: Arjun says he is Good, Noah says he is Good, therefore Evil is concentrated in Elena, Sam, and Theo, therefore this team is dangerous. Every step of that chain depends on believing two self-declarations. Arjun stating his alignment is the cheapest sentence in this game, and Noah declaring himself a Loyal Servant three times does not make it more verifiable — it just makes it more repetitive. The entire structure collapses if either claim is false, and Noah knows as well as anyone that it cannot be checked.

What bothers me most is the shape of the reversal, not just the logic. Noah accepted his seat on this team without objection, watched the discussion run, and then flipped at a moment designed to pressure Sam into a rushed revision — then nominated a replacement team that happens to put Noah's own name on it alongside the two players he just declared Good. Sam is right: that is opportunism wearing the costume of pure reasoning. If Noah were genuinely motivated by arithmetic alone, he could have proposed any combination of Arjun and Elena plus one unproven name. He chose himself.

And the arithmetic cuts both ways, as Sam noted. If we refuse to trust self-declarations — which is the correct posture — then Mission 1's clean result tells us less than Noah admits, and his own argument for benching Sam and Theo is no stronger than the argument he would make to bench himself if the seats were reversed.

I have seen nothing from Sam, Noah, or me that warrants a swap, and I have seen one genuinely suspicious behavior: Noah's last-minute flip designed to restructure the team in his own favor. My position is unchanged. I approve Sam, Theo, and Noah as proposed. Let us take the vote.

I am voting against Sam, Theo, and Noah as proposed. Sam's answer to my continuity question reframed the issue as rotation, but it did not address the specific risk from my seat. I know my own Mission 1 card was Success and I am loyal. That means both Evil players are among Arjun, Sam, Theo, and Noah. The proposed three-person team is drawn entirely from that pool, so from my perspective it necessarily contains at least one Evil player; if Arjun is loyal, it contains both. I cannot vote to hand a mission to a team I know has an Evil seat. I am not treating Noah's self-declaration as proof about Arjun — I am relying on my own card. The minimum correction is to include at least one Mission 1 participant. I would prefer myself because I can verify my own alignment, but I will support any revision that does not exclude both Arjun and me. Noah, since you made the arithmetic argument and Sam and Theo have now accused you of opportunism, can you state plainly whether you would vote against any final team that excludes both Mission 1 participants, including one that keeps you on it?

Elena asked me a direct question, so I will answer it plainly: yes. I will vote against any final team that excludes both Mission 1 participants — including a team that keeps me on it. If the final team is Arjun, Elena, and one other name, I vote for it. If it is Sam, Theo, and Noah, I vote against it, and my own seat on that team is not a reason for me to vote for it. That is the whole of my answer on the matter Elena raised.

Now let me answer Sam's and Theo's charge of opportunism, because it deserves a real answer rather than a shrug. I am not asking for the seat that suits me. I am asking for the one third name that follows from the arithmetic I laid out, and I want to show why it is not self-serving.

Here is the counting done carefully, with the limits of what I know stated first. I am a Loyal Servant. I know my own alignment is Good and no other role information at all — no sight of the Evil players, no card knowledge, no way to verify anyone's declaration. Everything below is counting on public statements, and the counting is worth nothing if the declarations are false, so I will separate the two cases.

Case one: Arjun and Elena are both Good, as they state. Then with me also Good, the three Good players are exactly Arjun, Elena, and me, and the two Evil players are exactly Sam and Theo. On that reading, a team of Sam, Theo, and Noah is not merely risky, it contains both Evil players and both Fail cards, and it fails with certainty. And the third seat on a revised team is not a free choice: Sam and Theo cannot both be on it, so the third name must be me. I am not nominating myself because it is convenient. Under the same arithmetic that says the current team contains two Evils, it says the only safe third name is me. If I were wrong about my own alignment, that team would be no worse than anything else available, because the failure would already be baked in.

Case two: at least one of Arjun or Elena is lying about being Good. Then the current team's probability of containing an Evil player is unchanged, and a team built around Arjun and Elena is no better than any other three. Here Elena's own statement is the one I weight, and she is the only person who can speak to her own card — and she has said her card was Success and that she is loyal.

So in every branch, a team of Arjun, Elena, and one other name is at least as good as Sam, Theo, and Noah, and in one branch it is the difference between a certain failure and a likely success. Sam's

On my final turn I will be clear. I will vote against Sam, Theo, and Noah as proposed. My objection does not depend on trusting Arjun's self-declaration. It depends on my own card: I was on Mission 1, my card was Success, and I know I am loyal. That means the two Evil players are among Arjun, Sam, Theo, and Noah. The proposed team is drawn entirely from that four-player pool, so from my seat it necessarily contains at least one Evil player, and if Arjun is loyal it contains both. Sam's answer to my continuity question acknowledged the risk but did not remove it; rotation is not a reason to field a team with no seat I can verify as Good. Noah has now answered my question directly: he would vote against any final team that excludes both Mission 1 participants, including one that keeps him. I take that as a commitment and expect him to honor it. I am not treating Noah's self-declaration as proof about anyone else, and I am not accusing Theo or Noah of anything beyond the structural problem. My position remains: I will support any final team that includes at least one Mission 1 participant, preferably me because I can verify my own alignment. The current team does not meet that standard, so I vote no.

Elena's objection deserves a direct answer on my final turn, and having heard her full case across two statements, I have updated my position.

Elena knows her own Mission 1 card was Success and knows she is loyal. That means both Evil players sit among Arjun, Sam, Theo, and Noah — exactly the pool this proposed team draws from. From her verified information, this team necessarily contains at least one Evil player. That is grounded in private card knowledge none of the rest of us can replicate, and I was wrong to treat the continuity argument as mere caution rather than a structural deduction.

I support revising this team to include at least one Mission 1 participant. Sam, as leader, should make that adjustment before the vote. I do not read Elena's concern as an accusation against anyone specific — it is a counting argument, and a sound one. The revision should address the composition problem without turning into an opportunity to scapegoat players who have been transparent. Sam proposed in good faith, Noah declared his information state openly, and I have been straightforward across both discussions.

My position: I will support a revised team that includes at least one Mission 1 participant, and I trust Sam to weigh this discussion and make the adjustment the table needs before we take the vote.

Third and final turn on this proposal, and my position has not moved — it is stronger now, not weaker.

First, the asymmetry Sam and Theo keep insisting on. They dismiss self-declarations as unverifiable. Elena's statement is not of that kind in the way they treat mine. 3. Team proposal and approval

The leader proposes a team of the required size and explains their choice. Players discuss the proposed team, and the leader may then keep it or revise it once. Every player votes on the final team. Ballots are revealed together. A strict majority approves; a tie rejects. After a rejection, leadership passes clockwise to a new proposal and discussion. The fifth rejection on the same mission ends the game in Evil’s favor.

4. Mission cards

Only team members submit secret mission cards. Good players must choose Success. Evil players may choose Success or Fail. Normally one Fail card fails the mission. Mission four in games with seven or more players requires at least two Fail cards to fail. Only the mission result and number of Fail cards are revealed; individual cards stay secret.

5. End of game and assassination

Three failed missions give Evil an immediate win. After three successful missions, the Assassin guesses Merlin from among the other players, excluding only their known Evil teammates. If the target is Merlin, Evil wins; otherwise Good wins. There are no further missions after either side reaches its win condition.

6. Discussion and record

Each team proposal is followed by a discussion. Before every speaking turn, the players who still have turns answer a private urgency poll or pass; the most urgent player speaks, with seeded tie-breaking. A speaker may yield the next turn to a player they directly asked a question. Each player has three turns per discussion, including declined turns. When every eligible player passes, the discussion ends. Each statement has at most 500 words. All statements are public. Team proposals, public approval votes, mission outcomes, and the assassination guess are recorded. Private role information, mission cards, and research belief surveys are not shown to other agents.
